concept.technique_name: Vedic Calendar Calculation (Month Key and Leap Year Counting)

examples.problem_statement: Using the Vedic Mathematics method for predicting days of the week, determine what day of the week was July 1, 1944. Follow these steps: 1) Take the last two digits of the year (44), 2) Add the number of leap years from 1901 to 1944 (including 1944 if it's a leap year), 3) Add the month key for July (0), 4) Add the date (1). Divide the total by 7 and find the remainder. Note: Since 1944 is a leap year but the month is July (not January or February), no adjustment is needed.

solution.operation: Take last two digits of year
solution.description: Start the day calculation by reducing 1944 to its last two digits, 44. The century is handled separately by this method, so only 44 enters the running total.

solution.operation: Add number of leap years from 1901 to 1944
solution.description: Count the years divisible by 4 from 1904 through 1944 and get 11. Each leap year added one extra day to the calendar since 1901, and 1944 itself is counted because the date asked for falls in July, after that year's 29 February.
July carries a month key of 0 in this system, so adding it leaves the running total at 44 plus 11 plus 0, which is 55.
Add the day of the month, 1, to the running total, bringing it to 56. All four ingredients of the method are now in the sum.
Divide the total 56 by 7 and keep only the remainder, since the weekday pattern repeats every 7 days. Seven goes into 56 exactly 8 times, so the remainder is 0.

solution.operation: Map remainder to day of week
solution.description: Read the remainder off this method's day code, which runs 0 for Saturday, 1 for Sunday and on to 6 for Friday. A remainder of 0 makes 1 July 1944 a Saturday.

examples.problem_statement: Find the day of the week for February 10, 1948 using Vedic Mathematics techniques.

solution.operation: Extract last two digits of year
solution.description: Reduce 1948 to its last two digits, 48, which is the starting number for the day calculation.
Divide 48 by 4 and keep the whole-number part, 12. That counts the leap years from 1901 up to and including 1948, each of which contributed an extra day.
February can take either key shown: 3 in an ordinary year and 4 in a leap year. 1948 is divisible by 4 and is not a century year, so the leap-year value 4 is the one carried forward.
Add the date itself, 10, with no adjustment; the day of the month always enters the sum unchanged.
Add the four ingredients together, 48 for the year, 12 for the leap years, 4 for February's key and 10 for the date, giving 74.
Divide 74 by 7 and keep the remainder, since weekdays repeat in cycles of seven. Seven fits 10 times with 4 left over, so the working day code is 4.
Dates in the 1900s carry a century code of 0, so adding it leaves the day code at 4. The step matters for other centuries, where the code is not zero.
Look the final code up in this method's day table, whose count starts at Friday for 0, so a code of 4 lands on Tuesday. 10 February 1948 was a Tuesday.

solution.description: Write the equation down as given, 5x + 3 = 4x + 7, noting that x terms sit on both sides and so cannot be read off directly.
Take 4x from both sides so that every x term collects on the left. This is the by-addition-and-subtraction move that keeps the equation balanced.
Simplify each side: 5x minus 4x leaves a single x on the left, and 4x minus 4x cancels on the right, so the equation is now x + 3 = 7.
Take 3 from both sides to strip the constant away from the x term and leave x standing alone.
Simplify both sides: the 3s cancel on the left and 7 minus 3 leaves 4 on the right, so x = 4.
Check the answer by putting x = 4 back into the original equation. The left side gives 23 and the right side gives 23 as well, confirming the solution.

solution.operation: Identify coefficients: a=5, b=3, c=6, d=-2
solution.description: Read the equation in the standard shape ax + b = cx + d. Here a is 5, b is 3, c is 6 and d is minus 2, and the minus sign belongs with d.
For an equation of this shape the Vedic shortcut hands x over directly as d minus b over a minus c, so no transposing back and forth is needed.
Put the four values into the formula: the numerator becomes minus 2 minus 3 and the denominator 5 minus 6, which is minus 5 over minus 1, so x = 5.

solution.operation: Identify values: a=1, b=3, c=-3, d=-5
solution.description: Match (x + 1)(x + 3) = (x - 3)(x - 5) against the pattern (x + a)(x + b) = (x + c)(x + d). That gives a as 1 and b as 3 on the left, while the two subtractions on the right make c minus 3 and d minus 5.

solution.operation: Apply formula: x = \frac{cd - ab}{a + b - c - d}
solution.description: Bring in the Vedic rule for this product pattern: x equals cd minus ab over a plus b minus c minus d. The brackets never have to be expanded.
Substitute the four values, so the numerator reads minus 3 times minus 5 less 1 times 3, and the denominator reads 1 plus 3 minus minus 3 minus minus 5.
Work out the numerator: the two negatives multiply to 15, and taking away the product 3 leaves 12.
Work out the denominator: subtracting the negative values of c and d turns them into additions, so 1 plus 3 plus 3 plus 5 comes to 12.
Divide the numerator by the denominator, 12 over 12, which gives x = 1 as the solution.

solution.result: \text{Multiply equation (1) by 3 and equation (2) by 2 to eliminate x}
solution.description: Plan the elimination: multiplying the first equation by 3 and the second by 2 brings both x coefficients to 6, which is what lets x be cancelled by a single subtraction.
Carry out those multiplications, scaling every term in each equation including the constants, to get 6x + 12y = 30 and 6x + 4y = 22.

Take 4 from both sides to get 2x = 6, then divide by 2 to get x = 3.
Check the pair in both original equations: 2(3) + 4(1) is 10 and 3(3) + 2(1) is 11, so x = 3 and y = 1 satisfies the system.

examples.problem_statement: Find the square root of 65536 using Vedic method.

Find the largest square that does not exceed the first group 6. That is 4, the square of 2, so 2 becomes the first digit of the root and the starting divisor, and 6 minus 4 leaves a remainder of 2.
